en: How does a car drive upside down on a ramp, then flip in midair and land on its wheels?
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's break this stunt down, step by step.
Tesla showed its new Roadster prototype doing exactly this in October, at a SpaceX test site in Texas.
Normally, an upside down car just falls off.
Gravity wins, and the tires lose their grip.
The trick is underneath.
Powerful fans suck the air out from under the car.
A skirt around the edges seals the gap, so outside air can't sneak back in.
Now the pressure under the car is low, and the air outside pushes it hard against the ramp.
It even works when the car stops.
But the moment the car leaves the ramp, air rushes in, and the grip is gone.
So it switches to cold gas thrusters.
Air is squeezed into high pressure tanks ahead of time.
When it needs a push, a valve opens and the gas blasts out of a nozzle.
Gas shoots down, so the car gets pushed up, just like a rocket.
Thrusters off, it falls faster and faster.
Both on, it still drops, but slower.
Push harder at one end, and the nose lifts.
That's how the car rotates in the air.
A spinning car won't stop by itself.
So just before it's level, the thrusters push the other way.
Then, right before touchdown, extra upward thrust slows the fall.
And the tanks hold only so much air, so every blast has to be planned.
Suction to stick, thrusters to flip, and a careful air budget to land.
Stay curious!
